Hands-on Exercise 5e - Treemap Visualisation with R

Author

Yang Yang

5.1 Overview

Treemap visualisation is useful when we need to display hierarchical data. Instead of showing values in a normal bar chart, a treemap uses rectangles. The size of each rectangle represents one quantitative variable, while the colour can represent another variable.

In this hands-on exercise, we use realis2018.csv, which contains Singapore private residential property transaction records in 2018. The hierarchy used in this exercise is:

  • Planning Region
  • Planning Area
  • Project Name

By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

  • import and clean private residential transaction data,
  • summarise transaction records into a treemap-ready structure,
  • design static treemaps using the treemap package,
  • compare different colour settings in treemap design,
  • build treemaps using treemapify,
  • create a simple interactive treemap using plotly,
  • add a small extension to compare resale condominium activity by planning area.
ImportantImportant

A treemap works best when the data has a clear hierarchy.
For this exercise, the hierarchy is geographic: Planning Region → Planning Area → Project Name.

5.2 Installing and Launching R Packages

Before creating the treemap, the required R packages need to be loaded. The main packages are treemap, treemapify, and tidyverse.

  • View
  • Code
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  treemap,
  treemapify,
  DT,
  janitor,
  plotly
)
NotePackage note

This version uses plotly for the interactive treemap instead of d3treeR.
d3treeR is not always stable because it is installed from GitHub, not directly from CRAN.

5.3 Data Wrangling

The raw transaction data is too detailed for a treemap. Each row is one transaction record, but a treemap needs summarised values by hierarchy.

The data is imported from the current exercise folder. Using list.files() avoids path errors when the website is rendered.

5.3.2 Cleaning the data

  • View
  • Code
realis2018 <- realis_raw %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>%
  mutate(
    project_name = as.character(project_name),
    planning_region = as.character(planning_region),
    planning_area = as.character(planning_area),
    property_type = as.character(property_type),
    type_of_sale = as.character(type_of_sale),
    no_of_units = as.numeric(no_of_units),
    area_sqm = as.numeric(area_sqm),
    unit_price_psm = as.numeric(unit_price_psm),
    transacted_price = as.numeric(transacted_price),
    sale_date = lubridate::dmy(sale_date)
  )

DT::datatable(
  head(realis2018, 12),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)

Column names are cleaned into a consistent format. For example, Project Name becomes project_name, and Unit Price ($ psm) becomes unit_price_psm.

5.3.3 Grouped summaries without the pipe

The basic idea is to group the transaction records by project and location, then calculate summary measures.

  • View
  • Code
realis2018_grouped <- group_by(
  realis2018,
  project_name,
  planning_region,
  planning_area,
  property_type,
  type_of_sale
)

realis2018_summarised_no_pipe <- summarise(
  realis2018_grouped,
  total_unit_sold = sum(no_of_units, na.rm = TRUE),
  total_area = sum(area_sqm, na.rm = TRUE),
  median_unit_price_psm = median(unit_price_psm, na.rm = TRUE),
  median_transacted_price = median(transacted_price, na.rm = TRUE),
  .groups = "drop"
)

DT::datatable(
  head(realis2018_summarised_no_pipe, 12),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)

This approach works, but it creates an intermediate grouped object. The pipe version is cleaner.

5.3.4 Grouped summaries with the pipe

  • View
  • Code
realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>%
  group_by(
    project_name,
    planning_region,
    planning_area,
    property_type,
    type_of_sale
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    total_unit_sold = sum(no_of_units, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_area = sum(area_sqm, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_unit_price_psm = median(unit_price_psm, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_transacted_price = median(transacted_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    total_unit_sold > 0,
    !is.na(median_unit_price_psm),
    !is.na(planning_region),
    !is.na(planning_area),
    !is.na(project_name)
  )

DT::datatable(
  head(realis2018_summarised, 12),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)
TipWhat can we learn?

The pipe version is easier to read because each operation follows the previous one.
This is useful for treemap preparation because the data needs to be grouped, summarised, filtered, and checked.

5.4 Designing Treemap with treemap Package

The treemap package is designed specifically for treemap visualisation. The key arguments are:

  • index: hierarchy of rectangles,
  • vSize: variable used for rectangle size,
  • vColor: variable used for rectangle colour,
  • type: how colour values should be interpreted.

5.4.1 Selecting resale condominium records

  • View
  • Code
realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(
    property_type == "Condominium",
    type_of_sale == "Resale"
  )

DT::datatable(
  head(realis2018_selected, 12),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)

The selected data focuses only on resale condominium transactions. This keeps the treemap closer to one property market segment.

5.4.2 Using basic treemap arguments

  • View
  • Code
treemap(
  realis2018_selected,
  index = c("planning_region", "planning_area", "project_name"),
  vSize = "total_unit_sold",
  vColor = "median_unit_price_psm",
  title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
)

This first treemap uses the hierarchy and two quantitative variables, but the colour setting is not yet ideal.

NoteReading the treemap

The larger rectangles represent projects with more units sold.
The colour is controlled by median unit price, but the default colour behaviour needs to be adjusted.

5.4.3 Working with vColor and type arguments

  • View
  • Code
treemap(
  realis2018_selected,
  index = c("planning_region", "planning_area", "project_name"),
  vSize = "total_unit_sold",
  vColor = "median_unit_price_psm",
  type = "value",
  palette = "Greens",
  title = "Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
)

With type = "value", the colour intensity reflects median unit price more directly.

5.5 Colours in treemap Package

Colour choice matters because a poor palette can make the treemap difficult to interpret. A diverging palette is more suitable when values have both negative and positive sides. For positive values such as unit price, a single-direction palette is easier to read.

5.5.1 The value type treemap

  • View
  • Code
treemap(
  realis2018_selected,
  index = c("planning_region", "planning_area", "project_name"),
  vSize = "total_unit_sold",
  vColor = "median_unit_price_psm",
  type = "value",
  palette = "RdYlBu",
  title = "Value Type Treemap: Resale Condominium, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
)

The value type treats the colour scale as a value-based mapping. Since unit prices are positive, the diverging palette may not fully use both ends of the colour range.

5.5.2 The manual type treemap

  • View
  • Code
treemap(
  realis2018_selected,
  index = c("planning_region", "planning_area", "project_name"),
  vSize = "total_unit_sold",
  vColor = "median_unit_price_psm",
  type = "manual",
  palette = "Blues",
  title = "Manual Type Treemap: Resale Condominium, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
)

The manual type maps the value range more directly to the colour palette. A single-colour palette is cleaner here because price is a positive continuous variable.

5.5.3 Small extension: using a custom teal ggplot version

  • View
  • Code
ggplot(
  realis2018_selected,
  aes(
    area = total_unit_sold,
    fill = median_unit_price_psm,
    label = project_name
  )
) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = my_dark,
    place = "centre",
    grow = FALSE,
    reflow = TRUE,
    min.size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    labels = comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Custom teal treemap of resale condominium projects",
    subtitle = "Rectangle size shows total units sold; colour shows median unit price",
    fill = "Median unit price\n(S$ psm)"
  ) +
  theme_yy

This extension uses the same treemap idea but applies the customised teal colour style.

5.6 Treemap Layout

The layout algorithm affects how rectangles are arranged. The treemap package supports different algorithms, including squarified and pivotSize.

5.6.1 Working with algorithm argument

  • View
  • Code
treemap(
  realis2018_selected,
  index = c("planning_region", "planning_area", "project_name"),
  vSize = "total_unit_sold",
  vColor = "median_unit_price_psm",
  type = "manual",
  palette = "Blues",
  algorithm = "squarified",
  title = "Squarified Treemap: Resale Condominium, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
)

The squarified layout tries to make rectangles closer to square shapes, which can improve readability.

5.6.2 Using sortID

  • View
  • Code
treemap(
  realis2018_selected,
  index = c("planning_region", "planning_area", "project_name"),
  vSize = "total_unit_sold",
  vColor = "median_unit_price_psm",
  type = "manual",
  palette = "Blues",
  algorithm = "pivotSize",
  sortID = "median_transacted_price",
  title = "Treemap Sorted by Median Transacted Price, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
)

The sortID argument controls the rectangle ordering when the selected layout supports sorting.

TipWhat can we learn?

Treemap design is not only about colour.
Hierarchy, size variable, colour variable, layout, and sorting all affect how the reader interprets the chart.

5.7 Designing Treemap using treemapify Package

The treemapify package allows treemaps to be created using the grammar of graphics. This makes it easier to combine treemap geometry with ggplot2 themes and scales.

5.7.1 Designing a basic treemap

  • View
  • Code
ggplot(
  realis2018_selected,
  aes(
    area = total_unit_sold,
    fill = median_unit_price_psm
  )
) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    labels = comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Basic treemap using treemapify",
    subtitle = "Area represents total units sold; fill represents median unit price",
    fill = "Median unit price\n(S$ psm)"
  ) +
  theme_yy

5.7.2 Defining hierarchy by Planning Region

  • View
  • Code
ggplot(
  realis2018_selected,
  aes(
    area = total_unit_sold,
    fill = median_unit_price_psm,
    subgroup = planning_region
  )
) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = my_dark, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(
    colour = my_dark,
    place = "centre",
    grow = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    labels = comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Treemap grouped by Planning Region",
    subtitle = "Subgroup borders separate the highest geographic level",
    fill = "Median unit price\n(S$ psm)"
  ) +
  theme_yy

5.7.3 Defining hierarchy by Planning Area

  • View
  • Code
ggplot(
  realis2018_selected,
  aes(
    area = total_unit_sold,
    fill = median_unit_price_psm,
    subgroup = planning_region,
    subgroup2 = planning_area
  )
) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = my_soft_teal, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = my_dark, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    labels = comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Treemap grouped by Planning Region and Planning Area",
    subtitle = "Two levels of subgroup borders make the hierarchy clearer",
    fill = "Median unit price\n(S$ psm)"
  ) +
  theme_yy

5.7.4 Adding boundary line and labels

  • View
  • Code
ggplot(
  realis2018_selected,
  aes(
    area = total_unit_sold,
    fill = median_unit_price_psm,
    subgroup = planning_region,
    subgroup2 = planning_area,
    label = planning_area
  )
) +
  geom_treemap(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = my_soft_teal, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = my_dark, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(
    colour = my_dark,
    place = "centre",
    grow = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    labels = comma
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Treemap with hierarchy boundary lines",
    subtitle = "Region and planning area boundaries improve readability",
    fill = "Median unit price\n(S$ psm)"
  ) +
  theme_yy

This version is visually cleaner because the hierarchy is easier to identify.

5.8 Designing Interactive Treemap

The original chapter uses d3treeR for interactive treemap design. To avoid installation problems, this exercise uses plotly, which is more stable in Quarto.

5.8.1 Preparing data for interactive treemap

  • View
  • Code
region_nodes <- realis2018_selected %>%
  group_by(planning_region) %>%
  summarise(
    label = first(planning_region),
    value = sum(total_unit_sold, na.rm = TRUE),
    color_value = median(median_unit_price_psm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    id = paste0("region|", label),
    parent = "Singapore"
  ) %>%
  select(id, label, parent, value, color_value)

area_nodes <- realis2018_selected %>%
  group_by(planning_region, planning_area) %>%
  summarise(
    label = first(planning_area),
    value = sum(total_unit_sold, na.rm = TRUE),
    color_value = median(median_unit_price_psm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    id = paste0("area|", planning_region, "|", label),
    parent = paste0("region|", planning_region)
  ) %>%
  select(id, label, parent, value, color_value)

project_nodes <- realis2018_selected %>%
  mutate(
    id = paste0("project|", planning_region, "|", planning_area, "|", project_name),
    label = project_name,
    parent = paste0("area|", planning_region, "|", planning_area),
    value = total_unit_sold,
    color_value = median_unit_price_psm
  ) %>%
  select(id, label, parent, value, color_value)

root_node <- tibble(
  id = "Singapore",
  label = "Singapore",
  parent = "",
  value = sum(region_nodes$value, na.rm = TRUE),
  color_value = median(region_nodes$color_value, na.rm = TRUE)
)

treemap_plotly_data <- bind_rows(
  root_node,
  region_nodes,
  area_nodes,
  project_nodes
)

DT::datatable(
  head(treemap_plotly_data, 12),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)

5.8.2 Plotting interactive treemap

  • View
  • Code
plot_ly(
  data = treemap_plotly_data,
  type = "treemap",
  ids = ~ id,
  labels = ~ label,
  parents = ~ parent,
  values = ~ value,
  branchvalues = "total",
  textinfo = "label+value",
  marker = list(
    colors = treemap_plotly_data$color_value,
    colorscale = list(
      list(0, my_light_teal),
      list(1, my_teal)
    ),
    showscale = TRUE,
    colorbar = list(title = "Median price")
  ),
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "<b>%{label}</b>",
    "<br>Total units sold: %{value}",
    "<br>Median unit price: %{color:.0f}",
    "<extra></extra>"
  )
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Interactive Treemap of Resale Condominium Transactions, 2018"
  )

The interactive treemap allows the reader to move through the hierarchy and inspect details by hovering.

5.9 Extra Analysis: Top Planning Areas

This small extension summarises the largest planning areas by total units sold. It supports the treemap by making the ranking easier to read.

5.9.1 Ranking planning areas

  • View
  • Code
planning_area_rank <- realis2018_selected %>%
  group_by(planning_region, planning_area) %>%
  summarise(
    total_unit_sold = sum(total_unit_sold, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_unit_price_psm = median(median_unit_price_psm, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_transacted_price = median(median_transacted_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_unit_sold))

DT::datatable(
  planning_area_rank %>%
    mutate(
      median_unit_price_psm = round(median_unit_price_psm, 0),
      median_transacted_price = round(median_transacted_price, 0)
    ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  class = "compact stripe hover",
  options = list(pageLength = 12, scrollX = TRUE),
  width = "100%"
)

5.9.2 Bar chart of top planning areas

  • View
  • Code
top_area_rank <- planning_area_rank %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

ggplot(
  top_area_rank,
  aes(
    x = fct_reorder(planning_area, total_unit_sold),
    y = total_unit_sold,
    fill = median_unit_price_psm
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    colour = my_dark,
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = my_light_teal,
    high = my_teal,
    labels = comma
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 15 planning areas by total units sold",
    subtitle = "This supporting chart makes the treemap ranking easier to read",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Total units sold",
    fill = "Median unit price\n(S$ psm)"
  ) +
  theme_yy

5.10 Final Takeaway

Treemap visualisation is useful when the data has a hierarchy and when both size and colour can carry meaning. In this exercise, total units sold controls the rectangle size, while median unit price controls colour intensity.

The treemap package gives a quick way to create traditional treemaps. The treemapify package gives more control through the ggplot2 grammar. The interactive version helps readers inspect the hierarchy more directly.

TipFinal takeaway

Use treemaps when the main question is about hierarchical composition.
For property transactions, treemaps help show how sales volume and price differ across region, area, and project level.

5.11 Reference

This exercise covered:

  • importing and cleaning realis2018.csv,
  • summarising transaction records for treemap design,
  • creating static treemaps using treemap,
  • adjusting vColor, type, palette, algorithm, and sortID,
  • creating ggplot-style treemaps using treemapify,
  • creating an interactive treemap using plotly,
  • adding a simple top planning area ranking as a small extension.
